effect: Crime now responds to policing and imprisonment. Before, police reached crime only through the clearance rate, which moved crime by -5.6% to +2.2% at most: doubling the police lowered crime by about 0.6%, while a 10-point rise in unemployment raised it 15%. Now each crime family's underlying level is also scaled by police capacity against day 0 (staffing, operating budget and stations, the same measure the game uses for clearance): violent crime by capacity^-0.5, property crime by capacity^-0.25, the criminal economy by capacity^-0.15, within 0.6 to 1.5 times. Capacity is about staffing^0.6, so per police officer this is about -0.3 for violent and -0.15 for property crime. A smaller incapacitation term uses the prison population against day 0 (violent and property crime, prison ratio^-0.1, within 0.85 to 1.15). A shrinking prison population (shorter sentences, fewer custodial sentences) raises crime a little the same way, and in a country with very few prisoners at the start a few cases move the prison term noticeably within its limits. Crime moves toward the new level at the game's own pace (about 5.5% of the gap a month). Examples: cutting police capacity by half raises violent crime about 41% and property crime about 19% through the police term alone; fewer police also clear and convict fewer cases, so the prison population falls over the following years and the prison term adds up to 15% more (at most 1.73 times in all); cutting the police operating budget to zero (capacity about 0.71 with the operations floor) raises violent crime about 19%. Real-world basis: estimated elasticities of crime to police numbers are about -0.3 for violent and -0.15 to -0.2 for property crime, and incapacitation effects are about -0.1 to -0.2 at ordinary prison rates. Day-0 effect: none (both ratios are 1 at the start).
